claims.statement: Dental radiography QA and repeat analysis are recognized audit activities, and EU law requires quality assurance and clinical audit for medical radiological practices.
Non-diagnostic positioning language does not settle MDR status; intended purpose and function control qualification and classification.
Retrospective dental images cannot be assumed anonymous merely because obvious identifiers are removed.
DICOM lowers an interface barrier but does not guarantee interoperability across dental sensors and PACS products.
Commercial incumbents already market image-quality checking and acquisition-time dental X-ray quality functions.
A narrow QA add-on would compete for budget with full imaging software priced at USD 199 monthly per location and with bundled vendor features.
Repeat rates vary from sub-1% in an experienced department to roughly 6-7% in a dental-school setting, making clinic-specific baseline measurement essential.
Poland has a substantial dentist base, but the number of compatible imaging locations and reseller-reachable decision makers is not established.
No public evidence reviewed establishes that a Polish or EU reseller will grant image, label, PACS and distribution rights for this product.
No public evidence reviewed establishes the module's MDR class, notified-body requirement or conformity cost under its final intended purpose.
A retrospective analytics and training wedge is less safety-sensitive than live accept-or-repeat guidance, but this is a staging inference rather than a regulatory determination.
Avoided retakes alone are not a conservative economic case; renewal may need to be justified by audit, training and reseller-service value.

contrary_evidence: Two named vendors already advertise functionality close to the original real-time quality-check thesis.
A mature department's 0.93% repeat rate demonstrates that high repeat savings are not universal.
DICOM is a standard, not a guarantee of operational interoperability or permission to access a vendor's system.
Dental morphology can support re-identification, so a de-identified pilot still needs careful privacy analysis.
Classification depends on actual intended purpose and function, making a formal opinion necessary before live use.
